implementation_notes: java.util.concurrent provides the pattern's parts in the standard library: BlockingQueue implementations such as ArrayBlockingQueue are capacity-bounded, put(e) blocks while the queue is full and take() blocks while it is empty, with offer(e) returning false and offer(e, timeout, unit) as the shedding and bounded-wait variants. Consumers are submitted to a fixed pool, so the queue bound plus the pool size together are the load-leveling controls; the hand-written wait/notify queue is never needed. Sentinels (poison pills) or interrupt-based shutdown end the consumer loops.
pitfalls: new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() defaults to Integer.MAX_VALUE capacity - an unbounded queue that looks bounded; pass the capacity explicitly.
A ThreadPoolExecutor with an unbounded work queue (the default for newFixedThreadPool) hides excess work inside the executor; the queue bound must sit in front of it.
put/take throw InterruptedException: swallowing it loses the shutdown signal, so the interrupt status must be restored or the loop terminated deliberately.
With several consumers the queue no longer preserves global order; ordering has to be keyed or the consumer count reduced to one.

variants.name: Virtual-thread consumers blocking on take() (Java 21)
variants.implementation_notes: JEP 444 makes blocking cheap: a virtual thread that blocks in BlockingQueue.take() unmounts from its carrier, so thread-per-consumer style code scales without an executor pool. The queue bound remains the real control - the JEP explicitly warns not to pool virtual threads to limit concurrency but to use constructs designed for it, such as semaphores, which here means the bounded queue itself. Choose this on Java 21+ where consumers are naturally written as straightforward blocking loops; the platform-thread pool remains appropriate for CPU-bound processing or older runtimes.
pitfalls: Virtual threads are not pooled: giving them a bounded pool re-creates the platform-thread limitation the JEP removes and is explicitly discouraged.
Blocking inside a synchronized block pins the carrier, so consumers that hold monitors across take()/I/O lose the scaling benefit; use ReentrantLock.
Because consumers are cheap, it is tempting to start far more than the dependency can serve: the downstream rate, not the thread count, still needs a bound.
